specPoints.text: describe tests for these cations: NH4+ using sodium hydroxide solution and identifying the gas evolved; Cu2+, Fe2+ and Fe3+ using sodium hydroxide solution

primer.text: From Flame Tests you already know one way to identify a metal cation: the colour it gives a flame. This note adds the solution route, where sodium hydroxide drops out coloured hydroxide solids, and finishes with the ammonium ion's own gas test.

lessons.title: Testing for metal cations
lessons.opening: Metal cations in solution are identified by the colours of the solids that drop out when a few drops of sodium hydroxide are added. Iron(II) gives a pale green solid, iron(III) an orange-brown solid and copper(II) a light blue solid. If nothing appears, the hydroxide may simply be soluble, or the solution may hold too few ions to show.
keyPoints: A few drops of sodium hydroxide are added first, and any precipitate is noted.
Iron(II) ions give a pale green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide.
Iron(III) ions give an orange-brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide.
Copper(II) ions give a light blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide.
No precipitate can mean the hydroxide is soluble, or too few ions are present.

low.restatement: Add sodium hydroxide drop by drop and watch the colour of any solid that forms: pale green means iron(II), orange-brown means iron(III), light blue means copper(II).
low.analogy: The three hydroxides are like three signature paints precipitating out of a clear varnish; the paint colour identifies which pigment, which ion, was dissolved in it.
low.examPointer: Use the full colour words, pale green, orange-brown and light blue, because bare green or blue is exactly what mark schemes decline to reward.

medium.restatement: A precipitate appears only when the metal hydroxide is insoluble, since the sodium hydroxide supplies hydroxide ions that meet the metal ions and build the solid. A blank result is not proof of absence: the hydroxide may dissolve away as fast as it forms, or the metal ion may simply be too dilute to give visible cloudiness.
medium.analogy: The reaction is like two crowds meeting in a corridor where only some pairs clump: the insoluble pairs form visible clumps, while compatible pairs drift through without ever gathering.
medium.examPointer: For no-precipitate questions, give both readings, soluble hydroxide or too little ion, rather than declaring the ion absent.

check.stem: What is added to test for metal cations in solution?

options.text: A few drops of sodium hydroxide solution
options.explanation: Sodium hydroxide supplies the hydroxide ions that form the coloured solids.

options.text: A few drops of dilute acid
options.explanation: Acid belongs to carbonate tests; the cation test uses an alkali.
The splint tests gases, not ions in solution.
That powder tests for water, not for metal cations.

check.stem: Which precipitate colour identifies iron(II) ions?

options.explanation: Iron(II) hydroxide precipitates pale green.
That is iron(III)'s colour.
That is copper(II)'s colour.
None of the three tested ions gives a white hydroxide here.

check.stem: Which cation gives a light blue precipitate?

options.explanation: Copper(II) hydroxide is the light blue solid.
Iron(II) gives pale green.
Iron(III) gives orange-brown.
Ammonium gives no coloured solid; its test releases ammonia gas.

check.stem: A solution gives no precipitate with sodium hydroxide. What are the two possible readings?

options.text: The hydroxide may be soluble, or too few ions are present
options.explanation: Both are the source's stated explanations for a blank result.

options.text: The solution is definitely pure water
options.explanation: A blank cannot certify the absence of everything; it only fails to show these solids.
A correct test can still give a blank for the two stated reasons.
Ammonium is one possibility among many and needs its own warm test to confirm.

check.stem: Why must exam answers state light blue, not just blue, for copper(II)?

options.text: Examiners are specific about the shade for the copper(II) mark
options.explanation: The source is explicit that light blue is needed to be sure of the mark.

options.text: Light blue means the solution is warm
options.explanation: Temperature plays no part in the colour of the precipitate.
Iron(III) is orange-brown; blue is not reserved for it.
The shade is the identity of the compound, not a concentration readout.

lessons.title: Test for ammonium ion, NH4+
lessons.opening: Ammonium ions cannot form a coloured solid, so their test works through a gas instead. Sodium hydroxide is added and the mixture is warmed, releasing ammonia gas, which turns damp red litmus paper blue. The ionic equation swaps one hydrogen ion for one hydroxide ion, giving ammonia and water.
keyPoints: Add sodium hydroxide and warm the mixture to release ammonia gas.
The ammonia gas turns damp red litmus paper blue.
The ionic equation is NH4+ plus OH- giving NH3 and H2O.
A faint cloudiness can still count as a positive result.
Ammonium is the cation NH4+, tested by the gas it releases with alkali.

low.restatement: Add sodium hydroxide to the solution and warm it: ammonia gas leaves the mixture, and damp red litmus paper turning blue confirms it. That gas is the ammonium ion's signature.
low.analogy: Warming is the door-opener here: without the heat the ammonia stays dissolved, and with it the gas walks out where the litmus can meet it.
low.examPointer: Name both the reagent and the warming, then identify the gas with the litmus result, because the test description needs all three parts.

medium.restatement: The hydroxide ion strips a hydrogen ion from NH4+ to make neutral NH3 and water, and warming pushes the ammonia out of solution as a gas. The litmus check closes the loop back to the gas tests, since ammonia is the only syllabus gas that turns damp red litmus blue.
medium.analogy: The reaction is a handover: hydroxide collects the spare hydrogen ion like a cloakroom attendant taking a coat, and the lighter guest, ammonia, leaves the room and announces itself downstairs.
medium.examPointer: Quote the ionic equation NH4+ plus OH- giving NH3 plus H2O, and link the gas to damp red litmus turning blue.

check.stem: How is the ammonium test made to work?

options.text: Add sodium hydroxide and warm the mixture
options.explanation: Both the reagent and the warming are needed to release the gas.

options.text: Add sodium hydroxide and cool the mixture
options.explanation: Cooling would keep the ammonia dissolved instead of releasing it.
Acid would protonate any ammonia made and stop the test working.

options.text: Add sodium hydroxide in the dark
options.explanation: Light conditions are irrelevant to this test.

check.stem: Which gas is released in the positive ammonium test?

options.explanation: Ammonia gas is the product the test looks for.
Hydrogen is the metal-acid gas, not this one.
Carbon dioxide comes from carbonates, not from ammonium ions.
Chlorine is a halogen gas unrelated to the ammonium test.

check.stem: How is the released gas confirmed?

options.text: It turns damp red litmus paper blue
options.explanation: That is ammonia's identifying result, linking back to the gas tests.

options.text: It bleaches damp blue litmus paper
options.explanation: Bleaching is chlorine's behaviour, not ammonia's.
The pop belongs to hydrogen.
Cloudy limewater identifies carbon dioxide.

check.stem: What is the ionic equation for the ammonium test?

options.text: NH4+ + OH- gives NH3 and H2O
options.explanation: The ammonium ion plus a hydroxide ion make ammonia and water.
Ammonium hydroxide is the dissolved form, but the gas-releasing step is the one the test cites.
options.misconception: dissolved form named as the gas step

options.explanation: That is the reverse, ammonia dissolving rather than leaving.
No hydrogen gas forms; the partner is the hydroxide ion making water.

check.stem: A very dilute ammonium solution shows only a faint cloudiness. What is the reading?

options.text: Still positive, small amounts give slight effects
options.explanation: The source notes that slight cloudiness can still indicate a positive result.

options.text: Negative, because cloudiness is never enough
options.explanation: A threshold that strict would contradict the source's guidance.
Nothing points to a different cation; faintness is about amount, not identity.

options.text: Invalid, the test must be repeated with acid
options.explanation: Repeating with acid would ruin the test rather than validate it.

glossary.definition: A positive ion, the species these tests identify.
The insoluble solid that drops out when sodium hydroxide meets certain metal ions.
The alkali reagent added to test for metal and ammonium cations.
The NH4+ cation, identified by warming with alkali and testing the ammonia released.
An equation showing only the ions that actually take part in the reaction.
